title: NK‐Cell‐Derived Extracellular Vesicles Engineered to Carry Senolytics Eliminate Chemotherapy‐Induced Senescent Osteosarcoma Cells

sections.abstract: Osteosarcoma (OS) is a type of bone tumour characterized by high risk of metastatic progression and recurrence after therapy. Traditional tumour treatment methods such as radiotherapy and chemotherapy can lead to the accumulation of senescent cells in tumours. Treatment‐induced senescence (TIS) can lead to incomplete tumour clearance and potential recurrence. Recently, the combination of chemotherapy drugs and senolytics drugs (‘one‐two punch’ therapy) has become a promising strategy for improved tumour treatment, but this method also faces challenges in terms of safety and targeting specificity. In order to further improve the efficacy of chemotherapy on OS, here we developed a senolytic drug delivery system based on engineered Natural killer (NK) cell‐derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) that can target OS cells. EVs were engineered to contain doxorubicin (Dox), termed iRGD‐EVs‐Dox, and used to induce cellular senescence in OS cells, followed by delivery of the Bcl‐2 family inhibitor ABT‐263 in similar engineered EVs (iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263), to specifically eliminate the senescent OS cells induced by Dox. Our results demonstrate that iRGD‐EVs have efficient targeting ability to OS cells and iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 effectively induced senolysis of Dox‐induced senescent OS cells in vitro and repressed tumour growth in OS cell xenograft mouse models. Taken together, our results demonstrate the therapeutic efficiency of using engineered EVs from NK cells to deliver first a chemotherapeutic agent to induce senescent OS cells followed by a senolytic drug to eliminate chemotherapy‐induced senescent OS cells, providing a novel strategy for more effective cancer treatment.
sections.introduction:
Osteosarcoma (OS) is the most common malignant bone tumour, mainly affecting children and adolescents (Ritter and Bielack 2010 ). At present, surgical resection combined with chemotherapy is the main treatment method, and doxorubicin (Dox) is one of the first‐line drugs for the treatment of OS, but with only partial effectiveness. After treatment with chemotherapy drugs such as Dox, both normal cells and remaining tumour cells can undergo senescence, a phenomenon known as therapy induced senescence (TIS) (Ewald et al. 2010 ; Prasanna et al. 2021 ). TIS recruits immune cells that can further promote tumour suppression through senescence‐associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors to slow down tumour growth; however, TIS also causes tumour cells to enter the cell cycle arrest stage and escape clearance by the immune system, as it creates an immunosuppressive microenvironment, especially in older individuals (Ewald et al. 2010 ; Prasanna et al. 2021 ). SASP factors are also able to promote angiogenesis and tumour growth. Incomplete clearance of senescent tumour cells may ultimately lead to tumour recurrence (Jochems et al. 2021 ; Kirkland and Tchkonia 2020 ). Thus, there is a significant need for novel strategies to eliminate senescent tumour cells (Fletcher‐Sananikone et al. 2021 ; Jochems et al. 2021 ).

Senolytics are a class of drugs that can specifically promote the apoptosis of senescent cells, such as multi‐kinase inhibitor dasatinib, natural compounds quercetin and fisetin, and the Bcl‐2 family inhibitor ABT‐263 (navitoclax) (Kirkland and Tchkonia 2020 ; Chibaya et al. 2022 ; Liu et al. 2022 ; Robbins et al. 2021 ). ABT‐263 can kill a range of senescent tumour cells without inducing cellular senescence (Short et al. 2019 ). In addition, ABT‐263 was shown to clear chemotherapy‐induced senescent cells, thereby reducing cancer recurrence and metastasis in a murine model (Demaria et al. 2017 ). However, ABT‐263 can also cause thrombocytopenia, an adverse effect that limits its application, due to its toxic effects on Bcl‐2‐expressing platelets (Demaria et al. 2017 ; Chaib et al. 2022 ; Lin et al. 2023 ). Therefore, here we explored the strategy of using extracellular vesicles (EVs) from nature killer (NK) cells to deliver ABT‐263 as the senolytic drug to eliminate senescent OS cells in order to reduce toxic side effects and increase tumour targeting ability.

EVs are nano‐sized, membranous structures secreted by most if not all cell types. EVs are comprised of vesicles with diverse size, content, and surface markers. In particular, EVs are comprised of exosomes, usually 30–50 nm in diameter and larger ectosomes, which are usually 100 to 1000 nm in size, as well as other types of larger secreted vesicles. All types of EVs contain various active substances, including nucleic acids, proteins and lipids, and can transmit information between cells to regulate pathological and physiological activities (Tian et al. 2023 ; Tenchov et al. 2022 ; Dorronsoro et al. 2021 ; Robbins et al. 2016 ). Compared with traditional drug carriers such as liposomes, EVs exhibit excellent biocompatibility, targeting ability, and low toxicity, making them excellent for delivery of therapeutic agents (Liang et al. 2021 ; Wang et al. 2021 ; Robbins and Morelli 2014 ). In addition, EVs can be modified to improve their targeting ability through expression or engineering of membrane proteins. EVs derived from NK cells were found to retain some characteristics of NK cells, having a certain targeting ability toward tumour cells and senescent cells. EVs from NK cells also carry various active substances that can kill the targeted cells, including perforin, granzyme, microRNAs (e.g., miR‐186, miR‐3607), and other active substances, thus exhibiting cytotoxic effects on various tumour cells and senescent cells (Wu et al. 2019 ; Neviani et al. 2019 ; Zhu et al. 2019 ; Zhu et al. 2017 ). Therefore, here we evaluated the use of NK cell‐derived EVs as drug delivery carriers to tumour cells and subsequently to senescent tumour cells.

Although NK cell‐derived EVs naturally have a certain targeting ability to tumour cells, after injection, the majority still accumulate in the liver or spleen, with only a small portion reaching to the tumour site (Wiklander et al. 2015 ; Huang et al. 2022 ). Therefore, we engineered EVs to increase their capacity to target tumour cells. Integrin αvβ3 is an important member of the integrin family and has been widely studied due to its critical role in tumour angiogenesis. Moreover, integrin αvβ3 is generally not expressed or expressed at a low level on the surface of normal tissue cells, but is overexpressed in tumour cells and tumour vascular endothelial cells (Desgrosellier and Cheresh 2010 ; Yuan et al. 2018 ). The iRGD (a tumour‐homing peptide motif) peptide binds specifically to integrin αvβ3 on tumour vascular endothelium and tumour cells (Lin et al. 2021 ; Wang et al. 2022 ). Thus, we engineered EVs to contain iRGD peptides on their membrane surface to improve targeting ability toward OS cells.

Also, the low isolation yield of EVs or exosomes greatly limits their application, and the amount of EVs produced by traditional 2D cell culture method is insufficient for clinical studies. Previous studies have established that 3D cell culture method can significantly increase the secretion and quality of EVs. Thus, here we applied a 3D cell culture system to increase cell number to increase the production of EVs.

Thus, in this study, our goal was to eliminate OS cells and senescent OS cells using modified NK cell EVs carrying either chemotherapeutic or a senolytic drug. EVs were loaded with either Dox or ABT‐263 using an electroporation method, and then the EV membrane was modified with tumour cell‐targeting iRGD peptides. A series of in vitro and in vivo experiments were conducted to evaluate their targeting ability and clearance effect on OS cells as shown in Figure 1 .

sections.methods:
The human OS cell line MG63, U2OS and the human Natural Killer cell line NK‐92 were obtained from Procell Life Science&Technology Co., Ltd (Wuhan, China). Human skeletal muscle cells HSkM was obtained from Shanghai Zhong Qiao Xin Zhou Biotechnology Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). MG63 cells and HSkM cells were propagated in DMEM (VivaCell, China) supplemented with 10% foetal bovine serum (FBS, VivaCell, China) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Solarbio, China). All cells were cultured in culture dishes and maintained in 5% CO 2 at 37°C.

1 × 10 7 NK cells were seeded into a 125 mL internal impeller culture bottle (CytoNiche Biotech, China), with 50 mL of EV‐free culture media (VivaCell, China). The rotation speed was set to 30 rpm, and performed fluid replacement treatment every 2 days. After 5 days of cultivation, collect the cell supernatant for EV isolation or store it in a −80°C freezer.

EVs were isolated using differential ultracentrifugation method (Federici et al. 2020 ). NK cells were cultured in EV‐free culture media for 48 h and the supernatant was centrifuged for 10 min at 300 g and 10 min at 2000 g to remove cells and large debris. Next, the supernatant was centrifuged at 10,000 g for 30 min and filtered through a 0.22 µm polyethersulfone (PES) membrane to remove large vesicles. The supernatant was then subjected to ultrafiltration in a tangential flow filtration (TFF) system using a 100 kDa cutoff TFF. Last, centrifugation was done at 100,000 g for 90 min with 70Ti rotor (BECKMAN, XPN‐100, USA). The pellets were then resuspended in PBS and centrifuged again at 100,000 g for 90 min. The EVs pellet was resuspended in 100 µL PBS. All of the above steps were performed at 4°C. The obtained EVs were quantified by BCA protein assay (Beyotime, China) and stored at −80°C.

All cells and EVs were lysed in 1×RIPA buffer with protease inhibitor PMSF. The lysate was mixed with loading buffer and boiled for 10 min. Proteins were separated on 7.5% and 12% SDS‐PAGE gel, transferred to PVDF membranes and blocked by 5% BSA for 1 h. The membranes were incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4°C. After being washed in 1×TBST, the membranes were incubated with HRP‐conjugated secondary antibodies at room temperature for 1 h. the PVDF membranes were visualized with an enhanced chemiluminescence system kit (Invitrogen, USA), and the grayscale of the strip was analysed by ImageJ. Primary antibodies used above include anti‐integrin αvβ3 (Abmart, China), anti‐Bcl‐2 (Santa Cruz), anti‐Bcl‐xl (Santa Cruz), anti‐caspase‐3 (Santa Cruz), anti‐CD9 (Santa Cruz), anti‐CD81 (Santa Cruz), anti‐TSG101 (Santa Cruz), anti‐Calnexin (Santa Cruz), and anti‐β‐actin (Proteintech, China).

The NK‐EVs (1 × 10 11 particles) were mixed with Dox or ABT‐263 (200 µg), placed at 4°C for 30 min, treated with an electroporation system, 300 V for four shock times, and then placed in a 37°C water bath for 30 min. Finally, free Dox or ABT‐263 was removed by ultrafiltration and the EVs loaded with iRGD (peptide sequence: CRGDKGPDC) using a commercially available kit (Echobiotech, China) following the manufacturer's instructions. First, 1.5 mL EVs (10 10 Particles/mL) and 100 µL lipid anchor‐targeting peptide solution were added to the reaction buffer. The mixture was incubated at 250 rpm at 25°C for 3 h and kept at 4°C for 24 h. Then, the samples were transferred to a 100 kDa ultrafiltration tube (Millipore, USA) and resuspended with 3.5 mL washing buffer, centrifuged at room temperature 4000 g for 30 min and washed and centrifuged again. The EVs were placed on the filter membrane, blown down gently and transferred to the empty EP tube. Morphology and size were observed by high‐resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM; HT7700, Hitachi, Japan) at 80 kV. The size distribution and particle concentration were analysed and recorded with the Nanoparticle Tracking Analysis software (NTA, Particle Metrix, Germany). The EV markers Calnexin, TSG101, CD81 and CD9 were confirmed by Western blotting analysis.

The amount of iRGD‐EVs‐Dox/ABT‐263 was measured and calculated from the standard calibration curve based on the absorbance at λ = 480 nm or λ = 320 nm measured by using a microplate Reader. The content/concentration of Dox/ABT‐263 was calculated according to the curve and the drug loading rate calculated. The loading efficiency (%) of Dox/ABT‐263 was calculated as follow W = W 1 − W 2 W 1 × 100 % where A is the loading efficiency (%) of Dox/ABT‐263; B is the original weight of Dox/ABT‐263; and C is the weight of Dox/ABT‐263 in the supernatants.

In six‐well plates, human OS cells (MG63 or U2OS cells) were cultured until the area of each well reached 70%–80%, and 50 nM Dox or iRGD‐EVs‐Dox was used to continuously treat OS cells in 5% CO 2 and 37°C incubator for 4 days. At Day 4, Dox was replaced with fresh media and cells were continued to be cultured for four more days with regular media changes every 2 days (Karabicici et al. 2021 ; Schnell et al. 2022 ).

Cellular senescence was assessed using the Senescence Detection Kit (Beyotime, China) per manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, the cells cultured in six‐well plates were washed once with PBS, and then 1 mL of β‐galactosidase staining fixative solution was added, left for 15 min at room temperature, and washed three times with PBS for 3 min each time. The SA‐β‐Gal staining solution was prepared under protection from light. To each well, 1 mL of the staining solution was added and incubated in a 37°C constant‐temperature incubator for 2 days under light protection. The staining was complete when the cells stained blue. The staining solution was replaced with PBS and photographed under a light microscope.

The prepared frozen slices were removed from the −80°C refrigerator and return to room temperature. β‐Gal fixative solution was added to ensure adequate tissue coverage and tissue was fixed at room temperature for no less than 15 min and then washed with PBS three times for 5 min each. The dyeing solution was proportionally configured avoiding light and the whole section was soaked in the dyeing solution for incubation at 37°C, again avoiding light.

The cellular senescence was also detected using CellEvent Senescence Green Detection Kit according to the manufacturer's instructions (Thermo Fisher, US). Cells were seeded into a 96‐well plate and allowed to attach by overnight incubation. After various treatments, cells were washed with PBS. The cells were fixed by adding 100 µL/well of Fixation Solution for 10 min at room temperature while protected from light. The cells were washed with 100 µL of 1% BSA in PBS per well to remove the Fixation Solution and prewarmed Working Solution was added at 100 µL/well of the 96‐well plate. After a 2‐h incubation and washing three times with PBS, staining was observed with a fluorescence microscope system (Olympus Corporation, Japan).

Cell proliferation was detected using a EdU cell proliferation assay according to the manufacturer's instructions (Thermo Fisher, US). About 3 × 10 4 cells were seeded in 24‐well plates and maintained for 24 h before the assay. A total of 500 µL EdU (10 µM) reagent was added to each well and incubated for 2 h to label the cells. After three washings with PBS, cells were fixed in a 4% paraformaldehyde solution for 10 min, permeabilized with Enhanced Immunostaining Permeabilization Buffer for another 5 min, and then incubated with the click‐reaction reagent for 30 min at room temperature in the dark environment. 1× Hoechst33342 reagent was used to counterstain the nucleus and staining result was then observed with a fluorescence microscope system.

The free ABT‐263 and iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 cytotoxicity in MG63 and senescent MG63 cells, and the free EVs and iRGD‐EVs cytotoxicity in MG63 and HSkM cells was determined using Cell Counting Kit‐8 (CCK8, SparkJade, China). Briefly, cells were cultured in a 96‐well plate at 10000/well in corresponding complete medium (100 µL) at 5% CO 2 at 37°C for 24 h. Subsequently, the culture medium in each well was replaced with 100 µL of fresh complete medium containing different concentrations of iRGD‐EVs (0, 20, 40, 80, 100, 200 µg/mL), free ABT‐263(1, 10, 20,40, 80 µM) and iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263(0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1 µM). After an additional 24 and 48 h of culture, the medium in each well was replaced with 100 µL of the CCK‐8 working solution. Then, after another 1 h of incubation, the viabilities of the cells in each well were determined by measuring the absorbance at 450 nm with a microplate reader.

A DiI Red Fluorescent Cell Linker Kit was purchased from Yeasen Biotechnology (Shanghai, China) and used to label blank‐EVs and iRGD‐EVs as described by the manufacturer. Any free dye was removed by centrifugation at 120,000 g for 90 min. MG63 and senescent MG63 cells were seeded into confocal dishes at a density of 3 × 10 4 cells/well and incubated overnight in an atmosphere of 5% CO 2 at 37°C. Cells were incubated with DiI‐blank‐EVs (5 × 10 8 particles/well) or DiI‐iRGD‐EVs (5 × 10 8 particles/well) for 2, 6 and 24 h at 37°C. Then, the cells were washed three times with 1 × PBS and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min. Subsequently, F‐actin was stained with Alexa Fluor 488 Phalloidin (Yeasen, China), the cell nuclei were stained with DAPI, and imaged using a confocal microscopy (ZEISS LSM 980, Germany).

Total RNA was obtained from cells using the Cell/Tissue Total RNA Kit (Yeasen, China). Reverse transcription was performed using an cDNA Synthesis Kit (Yeasen, China). Real‐Time PCR reactions were performed using an iCycler thermal cycler (Bio‐Rad Laboratories, Inc.). The gene‐specific primer sequences used are listed in Table 1 for p21, p27, Bcl‐2, Bcl‐xl, CXCL1, CXCL8, IL‐1α, IL‐1β, MCP1, MMP1, IL‐6 and GAPDH . The cycling parameters used for all primers were as follows: 95°C for 2 min; PCR, 40 cycles of 10 s at 95°C for denaturation, 30 s at 60°C for annealing and extension. All data were normalized to the expression of GAPDH.

The study protocol was approved by the Committee on the Ethics of Animal Experiments of Shandong First Medical University. Four‐ to six‐week‐old male nude mice (BALB/c) were purchased from Jinan Pengyue Experimental Animal Breeding Co. LTD and housed in a Shandong First Medical University specific pathogen‐free (SPF) animal room. Nude mice were injected subcutaneously with 5 × 10 6 U2OS cells. When the tumour volume reached 50 mm 3 , iRGD‐EVs‐Dox (2 mg/kg) was injected into the tail vein, and the changes in body weight and tumour volume measured every 3 days during the observation period. Two weeks later, the tumour bearing mice were euthanized and the tumour tissue was taken for SA‐β‐Gal staining. Tumour volumes were calculated using the following formula V = a b 2 2 where V is the tumour volume (mm 3 ), a is the tumour length (mm) and b is the tumour width (mm).

DiR‐labelled blank‐EVs and DiR‐labelled iRGD‐EVs (5 × 10 10 particles/animal, 200 µL) were injected into the mice via the tail vein. Then the mice after 24 h were sacrificed, and the fluorescence of the tumour resected in the mice was measured and compared by a small‐animal imaging system (IVIS) Lumina III system (Caliper, Hopkinton, MA, USA). In addition, the fluorescence intensity of the heart, liver, spleen, lung and kidney was measured.

OS tumours were established by subcutaneous injection of U2OS cells into BALB/c‐nu mice. After the tumours grew to a diameter of approximately 50 mm 3 , the tumour‐bearing mice were randomly divided into four groups ( n = 6) and injected with PBS, iRGD‐EVs and iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 (50 mg/kg) via the tail vein or ABT‐263 (50 mg/kg, dissolved in 60% Phosal 50 PG, 30% PEG400, 10% Ethanol v/v) via oral gavage. The mice were treated every 3 days for a total of six times, and were observed for 18 days. Changes in body weight and tumour volume were measured every 3 days during the observation period.

After the experiment, the tumour‐bearing mice were sacrificed, venous blood was collected, the tumours and major solid organs (heart, liver, spleen, lung and kidney) were harvested, and the tumours were photographed, weighed, fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde and embedded in paraffin. The tissue sections were stained with haematoxylin and eosin. Venous blood was centrifuged at 3500 × g for 10 min, and the serum levels of alanine transaminase (ALT) and creatinine (Cr) from the different treatment groups were measured to evaluate the biosafety of the drug loaded EVs.

In order to verify the reduced platelet toxicity of iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263, healthy non‐tumour bearing wild‐type C57BL/6J mice were divided into four groups with three mice each and injected with PBS, iRGD‐EVs and iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 (50 mg/kg) via the tail vein or ABT‐263 (50 mg/kg, dissolved in 60% Phosal 50 PG, 30% PEG400, 10% Ethanol v/v) via oral gavage. The mice were treated every 3 days for a total of six times, and were observed for 18 days. To perform platelet count in mice, blood was collected by superficial vessel puncture and move into anti‐coagulating tubes, and platelet levels were immediately measured using an automated haematology analyser.

Apoptosis in all tumour sections was evaluated using terminal deoxynucleotide transferase (TdT)‐mediated dUTP nick‐end labelling (TUNEL) staining, following the manufacturer's (Solarbio, China) protocol. Cell proliferation was assessed with an anti‐Ki67 antibody using immunofluorescence analysis. Then, sections were rinsed and blocked for 1 h at room temperature in blocking solution (PBS containing 5% BSA and 0.3% Triton X‐100). Sections were incubated overnight at 4°C with Ki67 antibodies, followed by incubation with Alexa Fluor 488‐conjugated AffiniPure Goat Anti‐Mouse IgG (Proteintech, China), at room temperature, for 1 h, and counterstaining with 4′,6‐diamidino‐2‐phenylindole (DAPI, Beyotime, China) to visualize the nuclei. Finally, the result of staining was observed with a fluorescence microscope system.

Statistical analyses were performed using Prism version 9 (GraphPad, USA). All data are presented as the mean ± SD of at least three samples. A t ‐test was used to analyse the differences between two independent groups, while a one‐way analysis of variance was used to analyse the differences between more than two groups. p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01 and *** p < 0.001.
sections.results:
Integrin αvβ3 is a member of the integrin family and a cell surface receptor that mediates cell adhesion. It plays a crucial role in the occurrence, development and metastasis of solid tumours. Related studies have shown that integrin αvβ3 is also highly expressed in OS. Firstly, in vitro cultured OS cells (MG63 and U2OS cells) were, respectively, treated with Dox (50 nM) to induce the senescence of OS cells (Figure 2A ). Then, we measured the levels of integrin αvβ3 in OS cells, senescent OS cells, and human skeletal muscle cells (HSkM cells) by Western blot. Compared with HSkM cells, the level of integrin αvβ3 was elevated in MG63 and senescent MG63 cells with similar results observed in U2OS cells and senescent U2OS cells (Figure 2B ). Since the iRGD peptide specifically binds to integrin αvβ3 and has been shown to increase drug accumulation when coupled or co‐delivered with particle surfaces, we linked the iRGD peptide to the surface of the EVs membrane to enhance targeting of OS cells.

Expression levels of integrin αvβ3 in OS cells and characterization of iRGD‐EVs‐Dox and iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263. (A) Osteosarcoma cells (MG63 and U2OS cells) were treated with Dox (50 nM) for 4 days and continued to be cultured without Dox for another 4 days to establish cellular senescence model of osteosarcoma cells. Cellular senescence was verified by SA‐β‐Gal staining, and the number of SA‐β‐Gal positive senescent cells was statistically analyzed under a microscope ( n = 6). Scale bar: 100 µm. ( B) Western blotting was performed to detect and compare the levels of integrin αvβ3 protein in human osteosarcoma cell lines (MG63, senescent MG63, U2OS, senescent U2OS) and human skeletal muscle cell line (HSkM). Gray analysis was performed by ImageJ ( n = 3). ( C) Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) was applied to detect the morphology of 2D‐EVs (EVs from 2D cell culture), 3D‐EVs (EVs from 3D cell culture), iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263, and iRGD‐EVs‐Dox. Scale bar: 100 nm. ( D) NTA detects the particle size of 2D‐EVs, 3D‐EVs, iRGD‐EVs‐Dox, and iRGD‐EVs‐Dox. ( E) Western blot analysis of EV marker proteins (Calnexin, TSG101, CD81, CD9) of 2D‐EVs and 3D‐EVs. ( F) Western blot analysis of EVs marker proteins (Calnexin, TSG101, CD81, CD9) of Blank‐EVs and iRGD‐EVs. ( G) The yield of EVs under 2D and 3D cell culture conditions. Data are presented as mean ± SD ( n = 3). * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, **** p < 0.0001.

Previous studies have shown that various stimuli, including physical, chemical and biological stimuli, can significantly increase the production of EVs. Providing certain physical stimuli, especially mechanical loads, can significantly increase the production of EVs (Debbi et al. 2022 ). We used a 3D culture system to cultivate NK cells in a dynamic state. Compared to 2D culture, the yield of EVs with 3D culture increased approximately 2.5 folds (Figure 2G ). 3D EVs also expressed the characteristic protein of regular EVs (Figure 2E ). TEM results showed that the morphology of 3D EVs was consistent with that of 2D EVs (Figure 2C ), with an average particle size of 138 nm for 2D EVs and 130 nm for 3D EVs (Figure 2D ), suggesting that there is no difference between EVs produced from 3D or 2D cultures.

We next loaded Dox or ABT‐263 into the EVs using electroporation method, and then modified the vesicles using a lipid anchor kit to attach the iRGD peptide to the membrane surface of the EVs (Yin et al. 2024 ). Western blot results demonstrated that iRGD‐EVs still contain key marker proteins of EVs (Figure 2F ). NTA analysis showed that the average particle size of iRGD EVs‐ABT‐263 was 183 nm, and the average particle size of iRGD‐EVs‐Dox was 155 nm. After drug loading, the particle size of EVs slightly increased (Figure 2D ). The TEM results showed that both iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 and iRGD EVs‐Dox had spherical vesicle structures, and electroporation did not damage the membrane structure of the EVs (Figure 2C ).

After loading Dox and ABT‐263 into EVs by electroporation, we used an enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assay reader to calculate the drug encapsulation efficiency. The results showed that compared with the iRGD‐EVs group, the UV‐Vis spectrum of iRGD‐EVs‐Dox showed a clear absorption peak from Dox at λ = 480 nm and the UV‐Vis spectrum of iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 showed a clear absorption peak from Dox at λ = 320 nm compared to that of iRGD‐EVs (Figure S1A,C ), indicating that iRGD‐EVs were successfully loaded with the each of the two drugs. The drug loading efficiency was calculated based on the absorbance of Dox at λ = 480 nm and ABT‐263 at λ = 320 nm, which were around 20% (Figure S1B,D ).

After treatment with free Dox and iRGD‐EVs‐Dox (50 nM) for 4 days, MG63 cells were further cultured in drug‐free medium for 4 days. The number of SA‐β‐Gal positive cells reached up to around 80% by either free Dox or iRGD‐EVs‐Dox (Figure 3A ), and fluorescent CellEvent staining for senescent cells was also positive after treatment with free Dox or iRGD‐EVs‐Dox (Figure 3B ), with significantly enlarged cell nucleus. In addition, after treatment with free Dox or iRGD‐EVs‐Dox, cell proliferation rate tested with EdU was significantly reduced (Figure 3C ), while the expression of p21 Cip1 and SASP factors was significantly upregulated (Figure 3D ). Similarly, after treatment of U2OS cells with iRGD‐EVs‐Dox, the number of SA‐β‐Gal positive cells reached up to 90% (Figure S2A ). These results indicate the successful establishment of an in vitro senescent OS cell model.

Establishment of an in vitro cellular senescence model for MG63 cells. (A) After treatment of MG63 cells with iRGD‐EVs‐Dox and free Dox, the number of SA‐β‐Gal positive senescent cells was statistically analyzed under a microscope ( n = 6). Scale bar: 100 µm. ( B) After treatment of MG63 cells with iRGD‐EVs‐Dox and free Dox, increased number of fluorescence positive cells was observed under a fluorescence microscope after CellEvent senescence assay. Senescent cells showed green fluorescence and the nuclei were blue ( n = 6). Scale bar: 100 µm. C . After treatment of MG63 cells with iRGD‐EVs‐Dox and free Dox, EdU measurement was performed, and the number of EdU (Alexa Fluor 488 azide labelled; green) positive cells were observed under a fluorescence microscope. Scale bar: 100 µm. ( D) statistical chart of EdU positive cells ( n = 6). ( E) RT‐qPCR assay of expression level of p21, p27 and a group of SASP factors ( n = 3). Data are presented as mean ± SD. *** p < 0.001, **** p < 0.0001.

We next evaluated the tumour‐targeting ability of iRGD‐EVs in vitro and tested whether iRGD‐EVs also have increased targeting of senescent OS cells. Blank‐EVs and iRGD‐EVs were labelled with fluorescent DiI and co‐incubated with MG63 cells and senescent MG63 cells for 2, 6 and 24 h. The results showed that while the uptake of Blank‐EVs and iRGD‐EVs by MG63 cells increased with time, the number of iRGD‐EVs entering the cells was significantly greater (Figure 4A,C ). Similar results were also observed in senescent MG63 cells, where iRGD‐EVs were more effectively internalized (Figure 4B,D ). Then, we examined the uptake effect of Blank EVs and iRGD‐EVs by HSkM cells. Compared to Blank EVs, there was no significant difference in the amount of iRGD‐EVs entering HSkM cells (Figure S3 ). Thus, iRGD‐EVs significantly increased the uptake of EVs by OS cells, but not by non‐tumour HSkM cells. These results indicate that modifying EVs with iRGD peptides can significantly enhance their targeting ability toward MG63 and senescent MG63 OS cells.

In vitro tumour cell targeting of iRGD‐EVs (internalization assay). (A) Confocal microscopy images of MG63 cells incubated with Blank‐EVs and iRGD‐EVs for 2, 6, and 24 h. ABT‐263 was initially used as an anti‐tumour drug, but had significant side effects. However, at low doses, it can be used as a senolytic drug to clear senescent cells (Fletcher‐Sananikone et al. 2021 ). We first tested the cytotoxic effect of free ABT‐263 and iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 on MG63 cells at different concentrations. It showed that at 1.0 µM, free ABT‐263 had less toxicity on MG63 cells compared to higher concentrations, and iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 also obtained similar result (Figure 5D,E ). Therefore, we applied 1.0 µM as the highest concentration for administering free ABT‐263 or iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 to senescent cells. Then, we tested the senolytic activity of free ABT‐263 and iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 on senescent MG63 cells at different concentrations. The CCK8 results showed that the survival rate of senescent MG63 cells decreased with the increase of ABT‐263 concentration (0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5 and 1.0 µM). After treatment with 1.0 µM concentration for 48 h, the cell survival rate was only 25% (Figure 5F ) and treatment with the iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 had a better effect on clearing senescent cells than free ABT‐263. Similarly, after treating senescent MG63 cells with free ABT‐263 and iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 for 24 h, SA‐β‐Gal staining results showed that the number of senescent cells gradually decreased with increasing drug concentrations (Figure 5I ), which was consistent with the CCK‐8 cell survival results (Figure 5F ). Western blot results showed that after treatment with ABT‐263, the expression of Bcl‐2 and Bcl‐xl was down‐regulated, and the expression of cleaved‐caspase3 was up‐regulated in both MG63 cells and senescent MG63 cells, indicating that ABT‐263 activated the apoptosis mechanism of cells (Figure 5G,H ). The PCR results showed that after administration, the expression of the CDKIs p21 Cip1 and p27 Kip1 and SASP related factors were down‐regulated, further confirming the decrease in the number of senescent cells (Figure 5J ). The above results indicate that iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 can effectively induce apoptosis of senescent MG63 cells more efficiently than free ABT‐263. Finally, we further validated the efficacy of iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 in clearing senescent OS cells using senescent U2OS cells (Figure S2 ).

After 2 weeks of treatment, the mice were euthanized and tumour tissues were collected and frozen for sectioning. Results showed that after treatment with iRGD‐EVs‐Dox, the SA‐β‐Gal positivity rate was significantly higher than that of the control group (Figure 6A ). Similarly, Western blot analysis showed that the expression of aging‐related markers p16 Ink4a and p21 Cip1 was increased and the number of Ki67 positive cells decreased post‐treatment (Figure 6B,C ), suggesting an increase in the number of senescent tumour cells. Importantly, the growth of OS tumour was inhibited (Figure 6D–F ), and there was no significant change in mouse body weight (Figure 6G ) following treatment with iRGD‐EVs‐Dox.

When the tumours reached to a volume of 300 mm 3 , DiR labelled Blank‐EVs and iRGD‐EVs were injected into tail vein. After 24 h, the mice were imaged using a small animal in vivo imaging system to track iRGD‐EVs (Figure S4 ). Subsequently, the mice were euthanized and their organs were taken to observe the distribution of Blank‐EVs and iRGD‐EVs. Fluorescence imaging and quantitative results (Figure 7A,B ) showed that EVs were mainly distributed in the liver and spleen, and the fluorescence intensity of iRGD‐EVs at the tumour site was significantly higher than that of Blank‐EVs. Then we evaluated the targeting ability of iRGD‐EVs on senescent OS cells. After establishing a senescent OS model in vivo with iRGD‐EVs‐Dox, iRGD‐EVs and Blank‐EVs were injected into tail vein, and their distribution was examined 24 h post‐injection. Results showed that the fluorescence intensity of iRGD‐EVs at the tumour site (but not at livers or other tissues) was significantly higher than that of Blank‐EVs (Figure 7C,D ). This indicates that iRGD‐modified EVs can effectively enhance the targeting ability of EVs toward both OS cells and senescent OS cells in vivo, which can effectively increase the accumulation of drugs at the tumour site.

Finally, we evaluated the ability of iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 to clear the senescent OS cells in vivo. After 2 weeks of treatment with iRGD‐EVs‐Dox to induce cellular senescence of OS cells, mice were randomly divided into four groups and intravenously injected with PBS, iRGD‐EVs (5 × 10 10 particles/animal), iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 (50 mg/kg), and ABT‐263 (50 mg/kg) via oral gavage. ABT‐263 was found in clinical trials to dramatically reduce platelets and severely affect the body's coagulation function, an adverse effect that makes it improper and dangerous to administer intravenously, and therefore it was orally administrated as a control in this experiment. The mice were administered with drugs once every 3 days, for six times. Compared to the PBS group, iRGD‐EVs inhibited tumour growth, indicating that iRGD‐EVs from NK cells had a basic therapeutic effect on the OS. However, treatments with either free ABT‐263 or iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 was more effective in inhibiting the growth of tumours (Figure 8A,B,D ) with a stronger therapeutic effect observed with iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263. TUNEL staining results show that positive staining area in the tumour tissue of iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 group was larger and had a higher number of apoptotic cells compared to the ABT‐263 group (Figure 8E ). Importantly, there was no notable loss in body weight observed in any of the four groups (Figure 8C ). Thus, these results verified that iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 was able to effectively target and kill senescent OS cells in vivo.

In order to evaluate the biological safety of engineered EVs, we used haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining to detect the histological changes of the most important organs (heart, liver, spleen, lungs, kidneys) and tumours in mice. Compared with the PBS group, no significant pathological changes were found in the main organs of the mice in the iRGD‐EVs and iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 groups, while the ABT‐263 group showed mild liver damage. In addition, compared with the PBS group, the other three groups showed varying degrees of tumour tissue apoptosis and necrosis, with the most severe pathology observed in the iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 group (Figure S5A ). Meanwhile, we also collected serum samples from mice to detect the levels of ALT and Cr, which are commonly used as biomarkers for liver and kidney injury. The results showed that the ALT levels in the ABT‐263 group were slightly higher while there were no significant changes in the ALT(alanine aminotransferase) and Cr (creatinine) levels in the other groups (Figure S5B,C ). Since it was shown that the main side effect of ABT‐263 is thrombocytopenia, we evaluated the potential platelet toxicity of ABT‐263 with or without being carried by EVs in healthy mice. Eighteen days of after treatment of mice with PBS, iRGD‐EVs, iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263, and free ABT‐263, it showed that ABT‐263 led to obvious reduction in the number of platelets in the blood of mice; in contrast, although iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 also caused platelet reduction, the level of reduction was much milder (Figure S5D ). The above results indicate that iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 has improved biological safety compared to ABT‐263.
sections.discussion:
Chemotherapy is an indispensable treatment method for patients with OS. However, the side effects conferred by the off‐target and high toxicity associated with the current chemotherapies significantly limit the practical application of chemotherapy drugs, leading to a high mortality rate in patients with OS (Wang et al. 2022 ; Wei et al. 2019 ). Therefore, more effective methods for delivery of chemotherapeutic agents with specificity to tumours is needed. In addition, since chemotherapeutic agents can also drive tumour cells into senescence instead of apoptosis, there is a need to also eliminate the treatment‐induced senescent tumour cells. Here, a promising new cancer treatment strategy of combining chemotherapy drugs with senolytics to treat tumours, termed the ‘one‐two punch’ therapy has been proposed. First, chemotherapeutics can be used to induce cancer cell senescence followed by treatment with a senolytics drug to eliminate senescent tumour cells (Jin et al. 2024 ; Wang et al. 2022 ). The current senolytic drugs, including the Bcl‐xl and Bcl‐2 family inhibitor ABT‐263, have shown the ability to clear senescent tumour cells in preclinical studies. However, the platelet toxicity of ABT‐263 limits its clinical application (Fletcher‐Sananikone et al. 2021 ). Nanoparticle‐based drug delivery can increase the delivery of chemotherapy drugs to the tumour area. However, the current traditional drug delivery systems have many drawbacks, such as low biocompatibility, high toxicity, and low delivery efficiency (Tenchov et al. 2022 ). EVs have emerged as efficient drug delivery carriers, exhibiting improved biocompatibility, targeting ability, low toxicity, and high transmission efficiency. Specifically, they do not have any side effects caused by drug aggregation, making them a promising drug carrier (Liang et al. 2021 ; Kimiz‐Gebologlu and Oncel 2022 ). Our current results also demonstrate that NK‐EVs have a cytotoxic effect on both OS and chemotherapy‐induced senescent OS cells. It has been proven that NK cell EVs contain cytotoxic components similar to NK cells, including perforin and granzyme, which are released into target cells after fusion with tumour cells through the vesicle membrane, and perforin forms pores on the tumour cell membrane, prompting granzyme to enter the cell to activate the apoptotic pathway, which ultimately leads to tumour cell lysis. NK cell EVs also express a variety of activating receptors (e.g., DNAM‐1, NKG2D and FasL) on the surface of NK cells, which can bind to the corresponding ligands on the surface of tumour cells and directly trigger apoptosis signals (Luo et al. 2022 ; Jong et al. 2017 ; Wu et al. 2019 ). Further, functional assays of human NK cell‐derived EVs had been performed with proteomics and miRNA analysis and the critical effectors (i.e., Fas ligand, TRAIL, and miRNA let‐7b‐5p) for the potent anti‐cancer function of NK‐EVs have been identified (Di Pace et al. 2023 ; Choi et al. 2020 ).

NK‐EV cytotoxicity should be some different between senescent and non‐senescent cells. Because senescent cells highly express a series of stress‐related ligands, such as MICA/MICB (NKG2D ligand), ULBP family proteins, and Fas receptors, due to DNA damage, oxidative stress and other stresses, which can be specifically recognized by activated receptors (such as NKG2D and FasL) on the surface of NK cell exosomes (Jong et al. 2017 ; Wu et al. 2019 ), thereby enhancing binding efficiency. NK cells and their EVs can also be recruited and activated by secreting SASP factors. Normal non‐senescent cells usually do not express or express at very low level of the above‐mentioned stress ligands, so NK‐EVs should have a weaker binding ability to non‐senescent cells, and the cytotoxicity effect should be lower than that of senescent cells. However, like many tumour cells, senescent cells are also able to develop increased immune evasion mechanism, which can lead to reduced NK‐EVs cytotoxicity. Therefore, in our study, NK‐EV was further modified by iRGD that have much stronger tumour‐targeting capacity, and used as a drug‐carrier at lower concentration to deliver highly cytotoxic senolytics.

Despite the improved drug delivery with EVs, the tumour‐homing ability of EVs is still limited. Therefore, here we also modified EVs with the tumour cell‐targeting iRGD peptide to increase their tumour targeting ability (Saifi et al. 2023 ; Wang et al. 2022 ). Previous studies have shown that iRGD is effective in improving tumour targeting and penetrating ability, and has been popularly applied to enhance the permeability and targeting of anti‐tumour drugs, thereby enhancing their anti‐tumour efficacy (Saifi et al. 2023 ). iRGD binds to integrin αvβ3 and αvβ5 receptors on the surface of tumour blood vessels receptors through RGD sequences, but these integrin receptors are not only present in tumour tissues, but can also be expressed at low levels in some normal tissues. For example, vascular endothelial cells involved in angiogenesis may express integrin receptors, which may lead to the accumulation of iRGD‐drug conjugates in non‐tumour regions and cause risks of cytotoxicity to normal tissues. However, the expression of integrin receptors in tumour cells is much higher than that of normal cells, and there has been no serious argument about its efficacy in related studies. Therefore, iRGD peptides preferentially target tumours, and NK cell‐derived EVs have some degree of natural targeting ability to tumours, further reducing the off‐target effect of iRGD peptides (St‐Denis‐Bissonnette et al. 2023 ). OS cells was shown to express high levels of the iRGD binding integrin αvβ3, and it is also noticed that expression of integrin αvβ3 protein is reduced in senescent OS cells compared to regular OS cells. Integrin αvβ3 protein play important roles in regulating the proliferation and migration of tumour cells, and it is possible that, when Dox‐induced cell cycle arrest and senescence significantly reduced cell proliferation and migration, the role of integrin αvβ3 protein in OS cells is limited, which is coupled with a decreased expression of integrin αvβ3 protein (Shi et al. 2022 ). However, the level of Integrin αvβ3 protein in senescent OS cells is still much higher than non‐tumour cells. After modification of EVs with iRGD peptide, the protein markers and morphology of EVs did not change, indicating that the modification did not affect their structure or function. In vitro and in vivo experiments confirmed that the iRGD modification improved the delivery efficiency and tumour‐targeting ability of EVs. Recent studies have reported that uPAR and PD‐L1 can serve as specific surface markers for some types of senescent cells (Amor et al. 2020 ; Amor et al. 2023 ; Wang et al. 2022 ; Majewska et al. 2024 ). Therefore, it may be possible to target EVs to specific senescent cell markers in future studies.

Here we have applied the method of electroporation for drug loading into EVs. Compared with popular traditional drug loading methods such as extrusion, freeze‐thaw, passive co‐incubation and other methods, electroporation and ultrasonication have been reported to have higher loading efficiency (Kimiz‐Gebologlu and Oncel 2022 ). Our study has tested and compared electroporation and ultrasonication methods of various settings, and found that electroporation at current setting is more effective for our system. However, in order to further improve the drug‐loading efficiency, other methods such as lipid‐based fusion (Piffoux et al. 2018 ) or a combination of different methods would be considered in our future studies. Therefore, a more efficient method would be desirable to improve drug loading efficiency into EVs. Also, there is need for improving the production of NK cell‐derived EVs for drug loading. Since previous studies have shown that various stimuli, including physical, chemical, and biological stimuli, can significantly increase the production of EVs or exsomes (Debbi et al. 2022 ), we used a 3D cell culture method to keep the cells in motion and increase the secretion of EVs. This led to an increased EV yield compared to 2D cell culture.

Large‐scale production of EVs is necessary for the application in clinical translation. For this study, the EV obtained from 3D cell culture is sufficient for the therapeutic application in our animal study, but for large‐scale clinical therapy, it will need a combination of multiple methods to further improve the yield of EVs, such as: cell bioengineering, bioreactor, chemical stimulation (TNF‐α, etc.), physical stimulation (hypoxia treatment, etc.), downstream optimization of extraction and purification methods, and improve the yield of EV (van Delen et al. 2024 ; Ghodasara et al. 2023 ). With the innovation of high‐efficiency separation and purification technology, the large‐scale clinical application of EV has become technically feasible and has broad prospects in the fields of clinical diagnosis, regenerative medicine and tumour treatment, but it also faces some challenges in clinical application. The heterogeneity of EVs (e.g., differences in size, composition) leads to batch‐to‐batch stability issues, and solutions include the establishment of uniform separation standards (e.g., ISEV guidelines). At present, the regulatory policies and standards for EV‐related products are not well‐established yet, and the production cost is generally high. Although the immunogenicity of EVs is low, the mechanism of their long‐term metabolism in vivo is still not well understood. Preclinical toxicology studies need to be strengthened to validate the safety through clinical data. However, with the continuous support of policies and the deepening of clinical research, EVs are expected to play an important role in the treatment of more diseases and become an important cell‐free therapy and diagnostic method. Future research should focus on solving technological bottleneck for EV production, improving clinical study design, and strengthening supervision and standardization to accelerate the realization of large‐scale clinical application of EVs.

Dox is an effective first‐line anti‐tumour drug with a wide spectrum of activity against solid tumours, and is widely used in the clinical treatment of OS. Also, Dox was found to be able to promote increased DNA damage and cell cycle arrest in OS cells, making them develop induced senescence. Therefore, Dox was chosen to induce the senescence of OS cells in this study (Mei et al. 2015 ; Uceda‐Castro et al. 2022 ). Here we used iRGD‐EVs‐Dox as a chemotherapeutic to reduce tumour growth and to increase the percentage of senescent OS cells. In vitro and in vivo results show that the senescent model was reliable for the study, with the proportion of senescent cells reaching up to about 90% in cell culture. The in vitro results also showed that at lower concentrations, treatment with iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 resulted in activation of the apoptotic mechanism of senescent cells and a subsequent decrease in the expression of SASP factors. Importantly, iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 effectively induced apoptosis of senescent OS cells induced by iRGD‐EVs‐Dox, and the clearance was better than soluble ABT‐263. The inhibition of tumour growth by treatment with iRGD‐EVs in vivo suggests that NK‐EVs retain killing activity similar to the parental NK cells. The ABT‐263 and iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263 groups significantly inhibit tumour growth compared to NK‐EVs and cleared senescent OS cells in the early stage of treatment. However, in the later stages of treatment, this anti‐tumour effect decreased, possibly due to an increase in the proportion of non‐senescent cells (SA‐β‐Gal negative) after the elimination of senescent OS cells. Therefore, the ‘one‐two punch’ therapy will require an optimization of the dose and treatment regimen of the combination to better exert its anti‐tumour effect. For future patients who possibly receive this long‐term one‐two punch treatment, because of the complication of this combined drug delivery system, the pathological examination (such as immunohistochemistry, tumour marker detection) and tumour imaging evaluation should be frequently performed, such as around every 2 or 3 weeks during the combination therapy and after the end of the therapy. The treatment regimen should be adjusted timely according to the treatment effect on the patients. In addition, according to the type of tumour, some other types of safe and effective chemotherapy and senolytic drugs can be screened and combined in the one‐two punch treatment method (Jaber et al. 2023 ; Saleh et al. 2020 ).

It is still need to be mentioned that, ABT‐263 may cause side effects such as thrombocytopenia, and in current study we have applied encapsulation of low‐dose ABT‐263 by EVs to possibly reduce its side effects. Future studies should evaluate long‐term hematologic toxicity of iRGD‐EVs‐ABT‐263, especially for potential clinical studies. Still, it would also be helpful to find a safer alternative drug if possible. Also, although RGD peptide can interact with integrin αvβ3 protein, it can only be applied to target tumour cells with higher level of integrin αvβ3 expression. Therefore, its efficacy against different types of tumour cells require further validation of integrin αvβ3 expression, or different types of targeting peptides can be applied according to the specificity of different types of tumour cells. In addition, this study was done with in vitro and murine models, which cannot fully simulate the complex environment in the human body, although they can help with mechanism exploration and preliminary validation of our approach. Future study is needed to further evaluate it in clinical settings.

In summary, based on the concept of the ‘one‐two punch’ therapy, we used NK‐EVs for encapsulation of a senolytic drug and established a safe and more effective drug delivery system based on tumour‐targeting EVs in an OS tumour model. Our approach has great potential for more effective treatment of OS and provides a guideline for the development of new tumour treatment approaches. It is important to note that chemotherapy, and possibly even NK‐EVs carrying chemotherapeutic agents, can also cause increased senescence of non‐tumour cells (normal cells). Further, in future research, we will aim to target the removal of senescent tumour cells while also removing senescent normal cell that accumulate with age. In this manner, we also can treat the complications caused by tumour treatments in addition to the tumour itself, preventing tumour recurrence, in order to achieve better and more comprehensive treatment for tumours.
